turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Aoife Murphy? In you come. Weight outside was 79 kilos, blood pressure 128 over 82, pulse 74.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Sorry, the telly out there was blaring and I couldn't hear myself think.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit. What's the problem?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's only the spots. My face is a war zone, but sure it's nothing. And the periods are all over the shop.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long, the spots?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Two years. The periods the same, about two years. I kept putting it off.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Coming every month?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Three, well actually four, the whole year. I'm not bothered.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain with them?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not a bit.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Heavy bleeding?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Light, when they show up. Hardly worth it.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any discharge, or burning when you pass water?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Waterworks are grand.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Chest pain? Short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bowels all right?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. No bother.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. I'll look.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Spots along the jaw, inflamed ones on the chin. Coarse hair on the upper lip and the chin. Tummy's soft, I can't feel a thing.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Working impression is polycystic ovary syndrome. Not confirmed.

[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fasting bloods Thursday morning. I'll start you on Dianette, the co-cyprindol, for the skin and the cycle. Scan only if it hasn't settled in three months. I'll see you in six weeks.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Dianette? Ah no. I don't want a pill. Um, I don't want hormones.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Reason?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): My mam had diabetes, the sugar, she's on tablets. And I've puffed up like a balloon, about a stone. Does that not count?
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): It counts. I didn't have it. Hair you've noticed, apart from what I see?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit on the lip, like a teenage lad. Everyone's hairy, it's nothing. Err, I haven't a clue when it started, last winter or the one before.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings I feel like a wet rag as well, but I've overdone it with college. Exams. Not a real thing.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything you're using on the skin?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the benzoil peroxide from the chemist. Five percent. A couple of nights a week, if I remember the spots.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Can't stand the smell.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): A few pints of a weekend. Not mad. The bus was a nightmare this morning, but anyway.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Scratch Dianette. I'm not starting the pill, or any hormone tablet, today. Your mother's diabetes and the weight change it.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bloods still Thursday, fasting from midnight, water only. Glucose and testosterone in with the rest. If the glucose is borderline we do a glucose tolerance test, not otherwise.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): And forget waiting three months. We'll book the pelvic ultrasound now.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So no tablet?
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): None today. If the testosterone is very high I might refer you to endocrine. Only then. We talk properly when the results are back.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Niamh, book those. Bloods Thursday morning with the nurse. First scan slot you have. And back to me in two weeks, not six.
[SEG0041] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Thursday at half eight for bloods, fasting, water only from midnight. Pelvic scan Friday week at two in the afternoon. Review here in two weeks.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Friday week, yeah? Do I have to drink litres of water for it?
[SEG0043] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): The letter will tell you that. Just no food before Thursday's bloods.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ease off the fizzy drinks and the late takeaways. It helps the weight. That's the lot.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not that heavy. A stone is hardly a crisis.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're 79 kilos and it's up. The bloods will talk.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): And the wet rag thing is only the exams. I'm grand.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noted. It still goes down.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the spots even go? Feels like a waste of a morning.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): No promises till the results. Questions?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've a lecture at four, so I need to hop.
[SEG0052] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): All booked, Aoife. Half eight Thursday, don't eat, water is fine. Scan Friday week at two. Back in two weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): On you go.

spec.situation: Young woman with acne and irregular periods for two years, some facial hair, weight gain; mother had diabetes; bloods and pelvic scan planned; contraceptive pill discussed, not started.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Morning tiredness is reported, but certainty is not certain; patient downplays it.
bad.text: tiredness (category=constitutional, status=present, frequency=in the mornings, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Periods occur only 3-4 times in a whole year / not every month.
Weight gain amount was about one stone.
Facial hair also present on the chin, not just upper lip.
Negative finding: no heavy bleeding with periods.
Negative finding: bowels all right / no bowel bother.

Doctor initially proposed starting Dianette (co-cyprindol) for skin and cycle and to scan only if not settled in 3 months, with review in 6 weeks, but this plan was changed after the patient objected.
Medication decision/change: patient declined Dianette/the pill/hormones, and doctor explicitly decided not to start any pill or hormone tablet today.
Reason discussed for not starting hormones: mother's diabetes and the patient's recent weight increase influenced the doctor's decision.
Follow-up timing was changed from six weeks to two weeks.

omissions.text: Initially the doctor planned to start Dianette/co-cyprindol for the skin and cycle and to do a scan only if it had not settled in 3 months, before this plan was changed after the patient objected.
Patient declined Dianette/the pill and said she did not want hormones.
Negative finding: no bowel problems/'bowels all right, no bother'.
The facial hair was not only on the upper lip; the doctor observed coarse hair on both the upper lip and chin, and the patient also described hair on the lip and chin ('like a teenage lad').
The doctor documented/acknowledged the patient's morning fatigue ('wet rag thing') despite the patient attributing it to exams.
